meta.subject: Anatomy
meta.scope_note: A must-do topic organised around one powerful, exception-light rule (function predicts nerve supply) plus one genuine, well-known exception (trapezius/CN XI) and a real clinical application (medial branch blocks) — scaled to 5 MCQs that cover the organizing principle, its application, its exception, and visual recognition, rather than padding with repetitive individual-muscle recall questions.
meta.note: Representative, high-quality MCQ family for this topic, not necessarily exhaustive. Dedup pass completed against this file's own question set — no duplicates found. Includes a genuine image-based question.

core_knowledge.definition: The muscles of the back are divided into two functionally and developmentally distinct groups with completely different nerve supplies: extrinsic (superficial) back muscles, which act on the upper limb and are supplied by ventral rami (anterior primary rami) of spinal nerves, and intrinsic (deep, 'true') back muscles, which act on the vertebral column itself and are supplied exclusively by dorsal rami (posterior primary rami).
core_knowledge.classification: Extrinsic back muscles are further split into a superficial group (trapezius, latissimus dorsi — supplied by cranial nerve XI and a plexus branch respectively, not typical dorsal rami) and an intermediate group (levator scapulae, rhomboids — supplied by plexus branches). Intrinsic back muscles form three layers (superficial/erector spinae, intermediate/transversospinalis, deep/short segmental muscles), all dorsal-rami-supplied.

structure_anatomy.extrinsic_superficial: Trapezius — supplied by the spinal accessory nerve (CN XI), with proprioceptive contribution from C3-C4 ventral rami. Latissimus dorsi — supplied by the thoracodorsal nerve (C6-C8), a branch of the posterior cord of the brachial plexus.
structure_anatomy.extrinsic_intermediate: Levator scapulae — supplied by the dorsal scapular nerve (C5) and direct branches from C3-C4. Rhomboid major and minor — supplied by the dorsal scapular nerve (C4-C5).
structure_anatomy.intrinsic_true_back_muscles: ALL intrinsic back muscles — including erector spinae (iliocostalis, longissimus, spinalis), transversospinalis group (semispinalis, multifidus, rotatores), and the short segmental muscles (interspinales, intertransversarii) — are supplied by the dorsal rami of spinal nerves, at the corresponding segmental level, with no exceptions.
structure_anatomy.key_rule: The single organizing rule for this entire topic: if a muscle moves the vertebral column itself (extension, lateral flexion of the trunk), it is intrinsic and dorsal-rami-supplied. If a muscle primarily moves the upper limb/scapula (even though it happens to attach to the back), it is extrinsic and supplied by ventral rami or plexus branches, NOT dorsal rami.

clinical.surgical_relevance: During posterior spinal surgery (e.g., laminectomy, spinal fusion), the dorsal rami supplying the intrinsic back muscles can be at risk — understanding that these muscles are dorsal-rami-supplied (not ventral-rami-supplied like most other muscles the surgeon might reflexively expect) is directly relevant to avoiding iatrogenic denervation.
clinical.back_pain_correlation: Facet joint and paraspinal muscle pain often involves the medial branch of the dorsal ramus at the corresponding level — medial branch blocks (targeting dorsal rami specifically) are a recognised diagnostic and therapeutic procedure for facet-joint-mediated back pain, directly built on this innervation pattern.

concept_blueprint.related_structures: The extrinsic-vs-intrinsic, ventral-rami-vs-dorsal-rami distinction is the single most tested organizing concept in this topic — nearly every question either directly tests this rule or tests a specific muscle's supply as an application of it.

mcqs.subject: Anatomy
mcqs.concept: Dorsal vs ventral rami supply to back muscles
mcqs.question: What single rule most reliably predicts whether a given back muscle is supplied by dorsal rami or by ventral rami/plexus branches?
options: If the muscle acts on the vertebral column itself, it is dorsal-rami-supplied (intrinsic); if it primarily acts on the upper limb/scapula, it is supplied by ventral rami or plexus branches (extrinsic), regardless of its position on the back
Any muscle located superficially on the back is dorsal-rami-supplied, while deep muscles are ventral-rami-supplied
All back muscles, regardless of function, are supplied by ventral rami
All back muscles, regardless of function, are supplied by dorsal rami
mcqs.correct_answer: If the muscle acts on the vertebral column itself, it is dorsal-rami-supplied (intrinsic); if it primarily acts on the upper limb/scapula, it is supplied by ventral rami or plexus branches (extrinsic), regardless of its position on the back

distractor_rationale.Any muscle located superficially on the: Gets the logic backwards on a technicality that matters: position (superficial vs deep) is NOT the determining factor — trapezius and latissimus dorsi are superficial but ventral-rami/plexus-supplied, while some intrinsic (dorsal-rami) muscles lie in intermediate or deep layers. Function, not depth, is the reliable predictor.
distractor_rationale.All back muscles, regardless of function: Overgeneralizes — the entire intrinsic (true) back muscle group is specifically dorsal-rami-supplied, a major exception this option ignores entirely.
Overgeneralizes in the opposite direction — trapezius, latissimus dorsi, levator scapulae, and rhomboids are all located on the back but are NOT dorsal-rami-supplied.

explanation.core_concept: This is the single fact that makes the entire back-muscle-innervation topic learnable as a system rather than a disconnected list — function (what the muscle actually moves) predicts nerve supply far more reliably than location (where the muscle sits) does.
explanation.why_correct: Muscles whose job is to move the vertebral column (extension, lateral flexion — the intrinsic/'true' back muscles: erector spinae, transversospinalis group, short segmental muscles) are supplied by dorsal rami, without exception. Muscles that happen to be located on the back but primarily move the upper limb or scapula (trapezius, latissimus dorsi, levator scapulae, rhomboids) are extrinsic muscles supplied by ventral rami, plexus branches, or cranial nerve XI (trapezius) instead — their back-surface location is developmentally coincidental to their limb-moving function.

why_others_wrong.Any muscle located superficially on the: Trapezius and latissimus dorsi are both superficial yet are NOT dorsal-rami-supplied — position on the back doesn't reliably predict nerve supply the way function does.
why_others_wrong.All back muscles, regardless of function: Fails to account for the entire intrinsic back muscle group, which is dorsal-rami-supplied without exception.
Fails to account for the extrinsic muscles (trapezius, latissimus dorsi, levator scapulae, rhomboids), none of which receive dorsal rami supply.

high_yield_facts: Intrinsic (vertebral-column-moving) back muscles = dorsal rami, always.
Extrinsic (limb-moving) back muscles = ventral rami, plexus branches, or CN XI — never dorsal rami.
This function-over-location rule is the fastest way to correctly assign nerve supply to ANY back muscle you're asked about, even ones not explicitly memorised.
explanation.clinical_correlation: This rule is what surgeons and anatomists rely on to predict which nerves are at risk during any given posterior approach — a superficial dissection reaching only trapezius/latissimus territory risks different nerves entirely from a deep dissection reaching the true intrinsic musculature.
common_confusions: Assuming 'back muscle' is a single homogeneous category with one nerve supply pattern — it's actually two developmentally and functionally distinct groups with completely different, non-overlapping innervation patterns.
related_concepts: Trapezius innervation (CN XI, an exception even within the extrinsic group)
Erector spinae segmental dorsal rami supply
Medial branch blocks for facet joint pain
exam_traps: Don't use superficial/deep LOCATION as your shortcut — always ask 'what does this muscle actually move?' first, since that functional question is what actually predicts the nerve supply correctly.
explanation.memory_aid: Moves the SPINE → dorsal rami. Moves the LIMB (even if it's sitting on your back) → NOT dorsal rami.
other_ways_this_is_tested: This organizing rule is applied directly in the specific-muscle-supply questions elsewhere in this set (trapezius, latissimus dorsi, erector spinae).
explanation.neet_pg_takeaway: Function predicts nerve supply for back muscles: vertebral-column-movers = dorsal rami (intrinsic); limb-movers = ventral rami/plexus branches/CN XI (extrinsic) — position on the back is not the deciding factor.
explanation.source_reference: Standard back anatomy — Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy, back chapter.

mcqs.learning_objective: Apply the function-based rule distinguishing dorsal-rami-supplied intrinsic back muscles from ventral-rami/plexus-supplied extrinsic back muscles.

mcqs.subject: Anatomy
mcqs.subtopic: Trapezius — the exception within the exception
mcqs.question: Trapezius is an extrinsic back muscle supplied by which nerve, distinguishing it from the pattern followed by most other extrinsic back muscles?
options: Spinal accessory nerve (CN XI), with proprioceptive contribution from C3-C4 ventral rami
Thoracodorsal nerve (C6-C8)
Dorsal scapular nerve (C5)
Direct dorsal rami at multiple thoracic levels
mcqs.correct_answer: Spinal accessory nerve (CN XI), with proprioceptive contribution from C3-C4 ventral rami

distractor_rationale.Thoracodorsal nerve (C6-C8): This supplies latissimus dorsi, a different extrinsic back muscle — not trapezius.
distractor_rationale.Dorsal scapular nerve (C5): This supplies levator scapulae and the rhomboids, not trapezius.
distractor_rationale.Direct dorsal rami at multiple thoracic: This describes the pattern for INTRINSIC back muscles, the opposite category from trapezius, which is extrinsic.

explanation.core_concept: Trapezius is genuinely unusual even among extrinsic back muscles — while most extrinsic muscles are supplied by named peripheral nerves arising from the brachial plexus (like latissimus dorsi and the rhomboids), trapezius's motor supply comes from a CRANIAL nerve, CN XI, reflecting its distinct embryological origin from branchial arch mesoderm rather than limb bud mesoderm.
explanation.why_correct: Trapezius receives its motor innervation from the spinal accessory nerve (CN XI), with an additional proprioceptive (sensory) contribution from the ventral rami of C3 and C4 — a nerve supply pattern shared with sternocleidomastoid (also CN XI-supplied), reflecting both muscles' shared branchial arch developmental origin rather than a typical limb-plexus origin.

why_others_wrong.Thoracodorsal nerve (C6-C8): The nerve supply to latissimus dorsi, a separate extrinsic back muscle with a typical brachial plexus-derived nerve supply, unlike trapezius.
why_others_wrong.Dorsal scapular nerve (C5): Supplies levator scapulae and the rhomboids — extrinsic muscles with typical plexus-branch supply, distinct from trapezius's cranial nerve supply.
why_others_wrong.Direct dorsal rami at multiple thoracic: This is the INTRINSIC back muscle pattern — trapezius, being extrinsic, does not follow this pattern at all.

high_yield_facts: Trapezius = CN XI (spinal accessory nerve) motor supply + C3-C4 ventral rami proprioception — NOT a brachial plexus branch, and NOT dorsal rami.
This is the same nerve (CN XI) that supplies sternocleidomastoid — both muscles share a branchial arch developmental origin.
Testing trapezius function (shoulder shrug) is a standard part of CN XI cranial nerve examination specifically because of this innervation.
explanation.clinical_correlation: Injury to CN XI (e.g., during neck surgery or lymph node dissection in the posterior triangle) causes trapezius weakness with shoulder drooping and winging of the scapula — recognising this connects a cranial nerve exam finding directly to a 'back muscle' weakness, a commonly tested cross-subject link.
common_confusions: Assuming trapezius, being an extrinsic BACK muscle, must follow the same brachial-plexus-branch pattern as latissimus dorsi, levator scapulae, or the rhomboids — trapezius's cranial nerve supply is the specific exception within the extrinsic group worth remembering separately.
exceptions: The C3-C4 ventral rami contribution to trapezius is proprioceptive/sensory only, not motor — motor function is purely CN XI's responsibility, a nuance sometimes tested directly.
related_concepts: Posterior triangle of the neck (CN XI's vulnerable course)
exam_traps: Don't default to 'brachial plexus branch' for every extrinsic back muscle — trapezius is the specific, frequently tested exception with cranial nerve (not plexus) supply.
explanation.memory_aid: Trapezius and sternocleidomastoid are CN XI's two 'accessory' territories — remember them as a pair.
other_ways_this_is_tested: Trapezius's CN XI injury pattern (shoulder drooping, scapular winging) is a classic cross-subject question connecting cranial nerve exam findings to back/shoulder muscle weakness.
explanation.neet_pg_takeaway: Trapezius, despite being an extrinsic BACK muscle, is supplied by the cranial nerve CN XI (plus C3-C4 proprioceptive fibres) — not a brachial plexus branch and not dorsal rami, making it an exception worth memorising on its own.
explanation.source_reference: Standard back/neck anatomy — Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy, back and neck chapters.

mcqs.learning_objective: Identify CN XI (spinal accessory nerve) as the motor supply to trapezius, distinguishing it from the typical brachial plexus branch pattern of other extrinsic back muscles.

mcqs.subject: Anatomy
mcqs.concept: Dorsal rami supply to erector spinae and deep back muscles
mcqs.question: The erector spinae group and the deeper transversospinalis muscles (semispinalis, multifidus, rotatores) are supplied by which nerves?
options: Dorsal rami of spinal nerves, at the corresponding segmental levels
Ventral rami of spinal nerves
Branches of the brachial plexus
The spinal accessory nerve (CN XI)
mcqs.correct_answer: Dorsal rami of spinal nerves, at the corresponding segmental levels

distractor_rationale.Ventral rami of spinal nerves: Ventral rami supply the extrinsic back muscles and the limbs/anterior trunk — the intrinsic muscles specifically follow the opposite (dorsal rami) pattern.
distractor_rationale.Branches of the brachial plexus: The brachial plexus supplies the upper limb and some extrinsic back/shoulder muscles, not the deep intrinsic back muscles, which have a segmental, non-plexus nerve supply.
distractor_rationale.The spinal accessory nerve (CN XI): CN XI supplies trapezius and sternocleidomastoid specifically — an extrinsic muscle exception, not the intrinsic back muscle group.

explanation.core_concept: Every muscle in all three layers of the true (intrinsic) back muscles — without exception — follows the same segmental dorsal rami supply pattern, making this one of the cleanest, most rule-based nerve supply facts in the entire upper/lower limb and trunk anatomy syllabus.
explanation.why_correct: The erector spinae (iliocostalis, longissimus, spinalis) and the transversospinalis group (semispinalis, multifidus, rotatores), along with the short segmental muscles (interspinales, intertransversarii), are all intrinsic back muscles supplied by the dorsal rami of spinal nerves at the corresponding vertebral level — a segmental pattern that holds true throughout the entire length of the vertebral column.

why_others_wrong.Ventral rami of spinal nerves: This is the extrinsic back muscle and limb/trunk pattern — the intrinsic muscles specifically do NOT follow this pattern.
why_others_wrong.Branches of the brachial plexus: The brachial plexus supplies upper limb muscles and specific extrinsic back muscles (latissimus dorsi, rhomboids, levator scapulae) — not the deep intrinsic musculature, which has a purely segmental, non-plexus supply.
why_others_wrong.The spinal accessory nerve (CN XI): CN XI's territory is limited to trapezius and sternocleidomastoid — it plays no role in supplying the intrinsic back muscles.

high_yield_facts: ALL intrinsic back muscles (all three layers) = dorsal rami, segmentally, no exceptions.
This is one of the most reliable, rule-based nerve supply patterns in the whole syllabus — once you know a muscle is 'true'/intrinsic back muscle, dorsal rami supply follows automatically.
The segmental nature (each level's dorsal ramus supplying the muscle at that level) is why localized back pain/spasm can sometimes be mapped to a specific vertebral level.
explanation.clinical_correlation: This segmental, dorsal-rami pattern is the anatomical basis for medial branch blocks — a diagnostic/therapeutic procedure targeting the medial branch of the dorsal ramus at a specific level to treat facet-joint-mediated back pain, directly built on this innervation fact.
common_confusions: Trying to assign individual, muscle-specific named nerves to intrinsic back muscles (the way extrinsic muscles each have a distinctly named nerve) — intrinsic muscles don't have individually named nerves; they simply follow the segmental dorsal rami pattern uniformly.
related_concepts: Medial branch blocks for facet joint pain
exam_traps: Don't overthink intrinsic back muscle nerve supply by trying to recall a specific named nerve — 'dorsal rami, segmentally' is the complete and sufficient answer for any intrinsic back muscle.
explanation.memory_aid: True back muscles = true to the dorsal rami, every single layer, every single level.
other_ways_this_is_tested: This segmental supply is the anatomical basis for the medial branch block clinical correlation question elsewhere in this set.
explanation.neet_pg_takeaway: Erector spinae, transversospinalis, and the short segmental muscles — the entire intrinsic back muscle group — are supplied by dorsal rami at the corresponding spinal level, without exception.
explanation.source_reference: Standard back anatomy — Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy, back chapter.

mcqs.learning_objective: State that all intrinsic (true) back muscles are supplied by dorsal rami at the corresponding segmental level.

mcqs.subject: Anatomy
mcqs.concept: Medial branch block for facet joint pain
mcqs.question: A patient with chronic lower back pain, worse with extension and rotation and localised to the paraspinal region without radiating leg symptoms, is being considered for a diagnostic nerve block targeting suspected facet joint pain at a specific lumbar level. Which nerve structure is the target of this procedure, based on the innervation of the paraspinal muscles and facet joints at that level?
options: The medial branch of the dorsal ramus at the corresponding (and adjacent) spinal level(s)
The ventral ramus at the corresponding spinal level
The sinuvertebral nerve
A branch of the lumbar plexus
mcqs.correct_answer: The medial branch of the dorsal ramus at the corresponding (and adjacent) spinal level(s)

distractor_rationale.The ventral ramus at the corresponding s: Ventral rami supply the anterior trunk, limbs, and extrinsic back muscles — not the facet joints or intrinsic paraspinal muscles, which are dorsal-rami territory.
distractor_rationale.The sinuvertebral nerve: The sinuvertebral (recurrent meningeal) nerve supplies structures WITHIN the vertebral canal (posterior longitudinal ligament, outer annulus fibrosus, dura) — a genuinely related but anatomically distinct target from the facet joints, which lie posterior/lateral to the canal and are supplied by the medial branch of the dorsal ramus instead.
distractor_rationale.A branch of the lumbar plexus: The lumbar plexus supplies the lower limb and anterior abdominal wall/pelvis, not the posteriorly-located facet joints or paraspinal muscles.

explanation.core_concept: Facet joints and the intrinsic paraspinal muscles overlying them share the same dorsal rami-derived innervation, which is exactly why a procedure targeting suspected facet-joint pain (medial branch block) makes anatomical sense as both diagnostic and therapeutic — and why understanding intrinsic back muscle innervation directly explains a real interventional pain procedure.
explanation.why_correct: The facet (zygapophyseal) joints, along with the overlying intrinsic paraspinal muscles, are supplied by the medial branch of the dorsal ramus — typically from the level of the joint AND the level above, since each facet joint receives dual segmental innervation. A medial branch block anaesthetises this specific nerve branch to determine whether it's the source of the patient's pain (diagnostic) and can be followed by radiofrequency ablation of the same nerve for longer-term relief (therapeutic) if the diagnostic block is successful.

why_others_wrong.The ventral ramus at the corresponding s: Ventral rami are not involved in facet joint or intrinsic paraspinal muscle innervation — this is exclusively dorsal ramus territory.
why_others_wrong.The sinuvertebral nerve: Supplies structures inside the vertebral canal (disc annulus, posterior longitudinal ligament, dura) — a related but anatomically and functionally distinct target from the facet joints themselves, which lie outside the canal.
why_others_wrong.A branch of the lumbar plexus: The lumbar plexus supplies the lower limb and anterior structures, with no role in facet joint or posterior paraspinal muscle innervation.

high_yield_facts: Facet joints + overlying intrinsic paraspinal muscles = medial branch of the dorsal ramus.

Each facet joint typically receives dual innervation — from the medial branch at its own level AND the level above — which is why medial branch blocks often target two adjacent levels for a single suspected facet joint.
This procedure is BOTH diagnostic (confirming facet joint as the pain source) and potentially therapeutic (via subsequent radiofrequency ablation of the same nerve).
explanation.clinical_correlation: This is a genuinely common, real-world interventional pain management procedure — understanding the underlying anatomy (dorsal rami supply to both facet joints and paraspinal muscles) is directly why the procedure is designed the way it is, not just an abstract anatomical fact.
common_confusions: Confusing the medial branch of the dorsal ramus (facet joints, paraspinal muscles) with the sinuvertebral nerve (intraspinal structures) — both are relevant to back pain but target anatomically distinct pain generators, and a real clinical workup needs to distinguish which is suspected.
related_concepts: Sinuvertebral nerve and discogenic pain (contrast target)
Segmental dorsal rami supply to intrinsic back muscles
exam_traps: When a vignette describes facet-joint-pattern pain (worse with extension/rotation, no radicular leg symptoms), don't default to a disc-related structure (sinuvertebral nerve) — match the CLINICAL PATTERN described to the correct anatomical target.
other_ways_this_is_tested: This procedure directly applies the segmental dorsal rami supply to intrinsic back muscles established in the direct-recall question earlier in this set to a genuine clinical intervention.
explanation.neet_pg_takeaway: Medial branch blocks target the medial branch of the dorsal ramus — the same nerve supplying both the facet joints and the overlying intrinsic paraspinal muscles — for diagnosing and treating facet-joint-mediated back pain.
explanation.source_reference: Standard interventional pain medicine anatomy — consistent with descriptions in pain medicine and spine surgery literature (e.g. Fischgrund's spine texts; interventional pain management references).

mcqs.learning_objective: Identify the medial branch of the dorsal ramus as the shared nerve supply to facet joints and paraspinal muscles, and its role in medial branch blocks.

mcqs.subject: Anatomy
mcqs.concept: Identifying extrinsic vs intrinsic back muscle layers on a dissection
mcqs.question: [Image: posterior dissection of the back showing, from superficial to deep: a broad flat muscle covering the upper back and shoulder region, then a muscle running from the lower ribs/lumbar region diagonally up to the humerus, then — after removal of both — a group of longitudinally-oriented muscle columns running parallel to the spine from the sacrum to the skull.] The deepest, longitudinally-oriented muscle group shown is supplied by which type of nerve?
options: Dorsal rami, segmentally
Ventral rami
The spinal accessory nerve (CN XI)
The thoracodorsal nerve

distractor_rationale.Ventral rami: Ventral rami supply the two more superficial muscles described (trapezius territory aside, which is CN XI) — the deep longitudinal group (erector spinae) specifically does NOT follow the ventral rami pattern.
distractor_rationale.The spinal accessory nerve (CN XI): This describes the FIRST (most superficial, trapezius) layer in the image, not the deepest longitudinal muscle group being asked about.
distractor_rationale.The thoracodorsal nerve: This describes the SECOND layer (latissimus dorsi, the diagonally-oriented muscle to the humerus), not the deepest longitudinal group.

explanation.core_concept: This image describes a classic back dissection sequence — trapezius, then latissimus dorsi, then erector spinae — and each layer has a completely different nerve supply, making 'which layer, which nerve' a natural and frequently tested image-based question format.
explanation.why_correct: The deepest, longitudinally-oriented muscle columns running parallel to the spine from sacrum to skull describe the erector spinae group — an intrinsic back muscle group, and therefore supplied by dorsal rami, segmentally, at each corresponding vertebral level.

why_others_wrong.Ventral rami: This pattern applies to some deeper structures elsewhere in the body but not to erector spinae, which is specifically dorsal-rami-supplied as an intrinsic back muscle.
why_others_wrong.The spinal accessory nerve (CN XI): This is the nerve supply to the FIRST/most superficial layer described (trapezius) — the question asks about the DEEPEST layer, a different muscle entirely.
why_others_wrong.The thoracodorsal nerve: This is the nerve supply to the SECOND layer described (latissimus dorsi, running diagonally to the humerus) — again, not the deepest longitudinal group being asked about.

high_yield_facts: Dissection sequence from superficial to deep: trapezius (CN XI) → latissimus dorsi (thoracodorsal nerve) → erector spinae (dorsal rami, segmental).
Each layer removed reveals a completely different nerve supply pattern — this progression is a common way to test whether all three patterns have been learned together, not in isolation.
The longitudinal, spine-parallel orientation is the key visual identifier of erector spinae specifically, as opposed to the more obliquely/diagonally oriented extrinsic muscles superficial to it.
explanation.clinical_correlation: Surgeons performing progressively deeper posterior spinal exposures encounter exactly this sequence of muscle layers and their correspondingly different nerve supplies — understanding which nerve is at risk at each dissection depth is directly relevant to surgical planning and nerve preservation.
common_confusions: Assuming that because all three muscle layers are visually 'on the back,' they share a single nerve supply pattern — the image specifically illustrates that they do not, each layer requiring separate identification.
related_concepts: Medial branch block (clinical application of erector spinae's dorsal rami supply)
exam_traps: Read the image description carefully for WHICH layer is being asked about — 'deepest' and 'longitudinal, spine-parallel' are the specific clues pointing to erector spinae and therefore dorsal rami, not the more superficial layers with their different nerve supplies.
explanation.image_clues: Key visual clues for erector spinae specifically: deepest visible layer (after removing the two more superficial muscles), oriented longitudinally/parallel to the spine (not diagonally toward the limb, as latissimus dorsi is), spanning sacrum to skull.
other_ways_this_is_tested: This image-based question synthesises the trapezius (CN XI), latissimus dorsi/extrinsic pattern, and erector spinae/dorsal rami facts established individually elsewhere in this set into one integrated dissection-sequence task.
explanation.neet_pg_takeaway: In a superficial-to-deep back dissection, the deepest longitudinal muscle group (erector spinae) is dorsal-rami-supplied — distinct from the more superficial trapezius (CN XI) and latissimus dorsi (thoracodorsal nerve) layers above it.
explanation.source_reference: Standard back dissection sequence — Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy, back chapter dissection images.
